title: What Jesus Really Meant by Becoming “Like Little Children” — And Why Most Adults Have Forgotten How to Come to Him
paragraphs: What Jesus Really Meant by Becoming “Like Little Children” — And Why Most Adults Have Forgotten How to Come to Him
Jesus was not telling you to become childish, naïve, gullible, or spiritually immature. He was exposing something adulthood teaches us to hide: our desperate need to receive what we can never earn.
There is something almost frightening about watching a little child reach for someone they trust.
No attempt to prove they deserve to be picked up.
Just two little arms reaching upward.
And perhaps that is exactly why the words of Jesus can become so uncomfortable once we really understand them.
Because somewhere between childhood and adulthood, many of us learned to stop reaching.
We learned how to smile while bleeding.
We learned how to say, “I’m fine,” when we were falling apart.
We learned how to make ourselves useful so people would keep us around.
Some of us even carried that same survival instinct into Christianity.
We pray, but sometimes we are secretly trying to impress God.
We serve, but somewhere underneath the service is the terror that maybe we are still not enough.
Promise God we will finally do better.
And when we fail again, shame whispers the same old sentence:
See? God must be tired of you.
Then Jesus places a child in the middle of grown adults and destroys the entire illusion.
The disciples had been discussing greatness.
“Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”
They were standing beside the Messiah...
It sounds ancient until you realize how painfully modern it is.
And Jesus answered their ambition with a child.
Matthew 18 says He called a little child to Himself and placed that child among them.
“Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.”
“ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία...”
ean mē straphēte kai genēsthe hōs ta paidia...
unless you become like the children...
This is not Jesus praising childish behavior.
And He immediately explains the point:
“Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”
Not pretending evil does not exist.
Jesus never commanded Christians to stop thinking. Scripture repeatedly calls believers toward wisdom, discernment, maturity, truth, and sober judgment.
The child in Jesus’ arms is not an advertisement for ignorance.
The child is a living confrontation with self-sufficiency.
And then another scene makes His meaning even more beautiful.
People began bringing children to Jesus so He could touch them.
The disciples tried to stop them.
Perhaps they thought Jesus had more important things to do.
More serious theological matters requiring His attention.
But Mark tells us something revealing.
When Jesus saw what they were doing, He was indignant.
Aphete ta paidia erchesthai pros me...
“Let the little children come to Me.”
Then Jesus spoke the sentence generations of Christians have repeated, sometimes without feeling its full weight:
“Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”
A child receives what another provides.
A child knows dependence in a way successful adults spend decades trying to escape.
And the Gospel begins exactly where human self-sufficiency ends.
You do not purchase the kingdom.
You do not impress your way into the kingdom.
You do not outperform your neighbor into the kingdom.
You do not accumulate enough religious achievements until God finally owes you salvation.
That is why grace can be so offensive to human pride.
We would almost rather earn something.
Because if we earned it, we could boast about it.
If we achieved it, we could control it.
If salvation were a ladder, we could compare ourselves with everyone standing beneath us.
But the Gospel removes the ladder.
At the foot of the cross, the billionaire and the beggar kneel on the same ground.
The preacher and the prisoner need the same blood.
The lifelong church member and the prodigal stumbling home from years of rebellion need the same Savior.
The respected Christian with a spotless reputation and the ashamed sinner who can barely lift his eyes toward heaven have only one doorway into reconciliation with God.
This is why Paul says salvation is by grace through faith, “not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Maybe that is why becoming “like a little child” becomes harder as life wounds us.
Wounded adults learn to say, “It doesn’t bother me anymore.”
Wounded adults often call isolation strength.
Children can run toward an embrace.
Wounded adults sometimes stand ten feet away wondering what the embrace will eventually cost them.
Maybe you learned early that people could leave.
Maybe someone who was supposed to protect you became the reason you needed protection.
Maybe love became something you believed you had to earn.
And without realizing it, you began treating God as though He were simply another unpredictable human being.
You promise Him improvement before approaching Him.
That is not how children come.
Children come because they need someone.
And sinners come to Christ for exactly the same reason.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Biblical childlikeness is not saying sin does not matter.
It is admitting that sin matters so much that you cannot rescue yourself from it.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who alone can save you from it.
And maybe someone reading this has spent years confusing spiritual maturity with needing Jesus less.
But genuine Christian maturity produces the opposite realization.
The deeper you walk with Christ, the more clearly you understand how desperately you need Him.
The mature believer does not eventually graduate from grace.
The mature believer becomes increasingly astonished by it.
You begin your Christian life saying:
And if God gives you eighty years of walking with Him, you may eventually whisper those same three words with tears because now you finally understand how true they were.
When I have sinned again and shame tells me to run away from God...
When death eventually stands at the door...
Maybe that is the child Jesus was showing us.
Someone who knows where to run.
And there is another detail in Mark’s account that is almost unbearably tender.
After Jesus defended the children, Scripture says:
He took them into His arms.
The King of kings had time to hold children everyone else considered interruptive.
The hands that would soon be pierced by Roman nails were placed upon little heads in blessing.
The One through whom all things were made stooped low enough for children to reach Him.
That is the heart of Christ.
And ultimately, that is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One came near to sinners.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The Shepherd went searching for sheep that wandered from Him.
The Author of life entered death.
And sinners who could never climb high enough to reach God discovered that God had come down to rescue them.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically good and merely needed encouragement.
He died because sin is real, judgment is real, separation from God is real, and we could not save ourselves.
But the cross declares something equally real.
And forgiveness is offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is what the child teaches us.
Perhaps your greatest obstacle to Jesus right now is not that you are too sinful for Him.
Perhaps it is that you are still trying to arrive carrying evidence that you deserve Him.
The carefully edited version of yourself you show everybody else.
Come like the person in the burning house who finally stops arguing with the rescuer and reaches for His hand.
Maybe you have been running from God for years.
Maybe you still attend church, but your heart has quietly moved miles away.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been watching.
Nobody knows what you have been hiding.
The nights when you stared into darkness wondering whether God still wanted anything to do with you.
Do not turn this article into another emotional moment you forget tomorrow.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Stop protecting the thing Jesus is calling you to surrender.
Not because your sin is small.
Not because you can rewrite your history.
Because Jesus Christ can redeem what your history tried to destroy.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.

Jesus rewrites lives by meeting guilty people with truth and grace, calling sinners to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming people who once thought their worst chapter had become their final chapter.
And perhaps the most childlike prayer you can pray tonight is not eloquent at all.
Someone else reading those words may finally find the courage to stop hiding too.
Because one day pride may tell you that you have to prove yourself again.
One day shame may tell you to stay away.
One day failure may whisper that Jesus could never want you back.
And on that day, remember the child.
It is helping biblical truth keep appearing in places where despair, temptation, confusion, compromise, and spiritual loneliness are already appearing every day.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So perhaps tonight, after all the noise dies down, you need to do something very small.
Stop promising God the improved version of yourself.
Because perhaps becoming like a little child was never about becoming less intelligent.

Perhaps it was about finally becoming humble enough to admit that beneath everything you have achieved, everything you have survived, everything you have hidden, and everything you are still trying desperately to control...
And the astonishing news of the Gospel is that the Savior who tells you to come like a child is the same Savior who opened His arms on a cross to bring repentant sinners home.
You spent years learning how not to need anyone. Grace begins when you finally reach up.
